segments.text: Taking a picture on your phone is usually straightforward.
You open the app, point the lens, and tap the button.
For most photos, the default settings work perfectly.
But specific environments require specific adjustments.
If it's dark outside, you turn on the flash.
If you are sitting high up in the stands at a game, you zoom in.
You don't have to touch these settings for every photo,
but knowing when to use them helps you capture exactly what you're looking for.
AI works the exact same way.
Depending on the app you use and your subscription,
you have three primary dials you can adjust.
The model, the thinking, and the research.
You won't need to tweak these for every prompt.
Understanding how they function simply gives you the control to get a better answer.
When you use an AI app, a large language model or LLM powers its answers.
Think of the LLM as the engine sitting inside the app.
When an app gives you the option to choose a model,
you are actually selecting which LLM engine you want to use.
Different engines come with different capabilities.
This graphic breaks down your first choice.
On the left, we have the everyday model.
This option is designed specifically for quick questions and simple tasks.
For example, you would use this model if you want the AI to suggest a funny movie to watch tonight.
On the right is the more capable model.
This engine is built to handle demanding tasks that require working through numerous details.
You would select this model to help you plan a summer business,
accounting for costs, pricing, and how many customers you will need to break even.
The rule of thumb here is simple.
Start with the default model and proactively switch to a more capable model
when your task complexity demands it.
Choosing a model changes the engine.
Adjusting the thinking setting changes how much time the AI spends working through your task.
Consider how a student approaches an English essay.
Before writing, they figure out the main points,
select examples to support them, and organize the structure.
AI doesn't reflect the way humans do.
But in this mode, it mechanically spends more time processing steps and weighing options
before it delivers a final answer.
Looking at our thinking options.
Less thinking means the AI spends minimal time working through the task.
This is useful for routine, uncomplicated work.
It's the right setting to turn a set of scattered group meeting notes
into a clear formatted checklist.
More thinking allocates more processing time for tasks that require deep analysis,
like coding, complex planning, and multi-step problem solving.
Use this setting if you need the AI to divide a week-long project among four people,
factoring in conflicting schedules and specific skills like video editing.
Intentionally give the AI more time to process whenever the task requires deeper working through.
The third and final option you can control is the research setting.
Basic knowledge retrieval is similar to ordering a fast food burger at a drive-through.
It's a simple, direct transaction that requires minimal prior context.
Buying a house requires a completely different approach.
You have to compare listing prices, evaluate neighborhoods,
and map out commute times across multiple data points.
AI's research mode mimics this extensive process.
It actively gathers and consolidates information from various websites,
so you can evaluate different options side by side.
This brings us to our research choices.
Regular chat can look things up, but it is meant for getting a basic answer to a direct question.
You use this to find out the total drive time between Dallas,
College Station, and Austin.
Deep research initiates a fuller investigation.
It compares information across many websites to build a fully sourced report.
This is what you need to compare undergraduate physics programs,
admissions requirements, and tuition costs between two specific universities.
Utilize deeper research specifically when you need to cross reference
and compare information from multiple sources.
This final chart summarizes the three distinct choices you now control.
The model, the thinking, and the research.
You won't need them every time.
Use them when the work demands more.
